keyVerseText: And the king of Assyria sent Tartan and Rabsaris and Rabshakeh from Lachish to king Hezekiah with a great host against Jerusalem. And they went up and came to Jerusalem. And when they were come up, they came and stood by the conduit of the upper pool, which is in the highway of the fuller's field. great: Heb. heavy
rootMeaning: The Hebrew word תַּרְתָּן (Tartân) is of foreign derivation, borrowed from the Assyrian title tartânu or turtânu, signifying a high-ranking military officer. Unlike a common noun, it functions as a specific title denoting authority and command, literally referring to a field marshal or general. This root sense highlights the word's role not merely as a name but as an official military rank, emphasizing leadership and power within the Assyrian army.
usageInScripture: The term תַּרְתָּן appears only twice in Scripture, consistently translated as 'Tartan' or 'that Tartan,' reflecting its status as a proper title rather than a descriptive noun. Both occurrences relate to the Assyrian military context, underscoring the word's use to identify a particular Assyrian general or commander. This consistency reveals the term's specificity and importance in describing the Assyrian hierarchy during pivotal interactions with Israel and Judah.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תַּרְתָּן as a title of Assyrian military leadership enriches our grasp of the biblical narrative concerning God's sovereignty over earthly powers. The presence of such a figure in Scripture reminds believers that even the mightiest human authorities operate under God's providential control. This word draws attention to the reality of spiritual warfare and the challenge posed by hostile powers to God's people, ultimately pointing to Christ's supreme authority over all rulers. Recognizing the Assyrian commander as a tangible representation of opposition encourages faithfulness and trust in God's deliverance.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Kings 18:17, the king of Assyria sends 'Tartan' alongside other officials to confront King Hezekiah, highlighting the military pressure on Jerusalem. The use of תַּרְתָּן here identifies a key general leading the Assyrian forces, emphasizing the seriousness and organized nature of the threat. This title contributes to the verse by portraying the Assyrian delegation as authoritative and formidable, setting the stage for the dramatic reliance on God's protection in the face of overwhelming human opposition.
